what_it_does: IBM's Telum II is a high-performance processor chip made at Samsung's 5 nanometer process node (each transistor is about 50,000 times smaller than a grain of salt). Building such a chip requires solving an impossible-seeming puzzle: optimizing power consumption, speed, area, and reliability all at once, while managing millions of design decisions across the chip's components. This paper describes how IBM solved this by redesigning the foundational building blocks (standard cells—the tiny repeated circuits that make up 99% of the chip) jointly with the manufacturing process itself, and by running dozens of design teams in parallel rather than in sequence, so that memory arrays, registers, analog circuits, and custom logic all get optimized together from day one instead of being bolted together at the end.
